strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: improving open reward models via preference data quality rather than only architecture or loss changes.

The empirical results are strong and broad: Skywork-Reward-V2 is evaluated across seven reward-model benchmarks, including RewardBench v2, PPE, RMB, RM-Bench, and JudgeBench, with large reported gains over strong open and proprietary baselines.
The work provides a practically useful suite of reward models across several sizes, including small models that reportedly outperform much larger prior reward models on average.

The proposed two-stage human-AI curation pipeline is sensible and well motivated, combining human-verified seed data, LLM-assisted annotation, adaptive retrieval, and consistency-based large-scale filtering.

The ablations are useful: the paper compares uncurated scaling, filtered data, corrected/flipped data, LLM-only curation, human curation, adaptive retrieval, and variants of the human annotation protocol.
The paper clearly identifies over-optimization to RewardBench and argues for broader reward-model evaluation, which is valuable for the field.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a major concern. The paper does not provide enough concrete information about the composition of SynPref-40M, the number of human-labeled examples, annotator qualifications, agreement rates, quality-control statistics, annotation costs, or detailed prompt templates to reproduce the pipeline.

The central data contribution is hard to independently assess. It is unclear whether the full SynPref-40M or the curated 26M subset will be released, and without the data the main scientific contribution becomes difficult to verify.

Benchmark contamination remains a serious risk. The paper uses a 13-gram overlap against first-turn prompts, but the training mixture is assembled from many public preference sources and LLM-generated labels; this decontamination procedure may miss paraphrases, multi-turn overlap, benchmark-derived responses, or contamination through LLM annotators.

The evaluation is benchmark-heavy and lacks convincing downstream RLHF/policy optimization experiments. Best-of-N results are useful, but they do not fully establish that the reward models improve actual policy training or avoid reward hacking in realistic RLHF settings.

Several parts of the method are underspecified or circular. The “gold reward model” is trained from human-verified data and then used to filter additional data, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze how errors or biases in this gold model propagate into the final dataset.

The flipped discarded-data result is intriguing but not adequately justified. Simply reversing discarded preferences could introduce systematic noise, and the paper acknowledges that this pool was not rigorously verified.

The method depends heavily on frontier LLMs and external tools during annotation, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze cost, availability, bias, privacy, licensing, or whether similar results hold with reproducible open annotators.
Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially broad statements about capturing nuanced human preferences and reward models becoming foundational AI infrastructure.

Human-subject and data-governance details are thin. Compensation, annotator welfare, demographic diversity, privacy handling, and potential exposure to harmful content are not discussed in enough depth for a large-scale preference annotation effort.
The ablations are limited to early-stage or partial-pipeline settings, so they do not fully isolate which components matter at the final 26M/40M scale.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: improving open reward models through preference-data quality rather than only architecture or loss changes.
The claimed empirical gains are large and are reported across several relevant reward-model benchmarks, including style-bias, correctness, and best-of-N evaluations.
The paper includes some useful ablations suggesting that human curation, preference attributes, verification protocols, and adaptive retrieval each contribute to performance.
The release of multiple model sizes, if actually accompanied by usable artifacts and sufficient documentation, could be valuable to the community.
weaknesses: The central contribution is insufficiently reproducible. Key details of the 40M-pair mixture, source composition, exact filtering decisions, annotation prompts, human annotation volume, annotator qualifications, cost, agreement, and quality-control statistics are missing or too vague for independent assessment.

The evaluation is at high risk of benchmark overfitting or contamination. The authors repeatedly use public benchmarks to motivate, track, and compare progress, and even report training curves using average benchmark scores. The decontamination procedure is shallow, relying on first-turn 13-gram overlap, which is not convincing for preference pairs, generated variants, or semantically similar examples.

The main claims about modeling human preferences are much stronger than the evidence. Most evaluation is benchmark accuracy; there is no convincing downstream RLHF or policy-optimization evaluation showing that these reward models actually improve aligned generation in realistic use.

The data-curation pipeline is opaque and partly circular: reward models and LLM judges are used to select, relabel, flip, and validate data, then benchmark gains are used as evidence that the pipeline corrected preferences. The paper does not provide enough human audit evidence that flipped or retained labels are actually correct.

Human annotation is presented as a major quality source, but the paper lacks basic annotation science: no inter-annotator agreement, no blind adjudication protocol, no demographic or expertise information, no error analysis, and authors themselves participated in later annotation stages, raising bias concerns.

The comparisons are not fully satisfactory. Several baselines have missing entries, different model sizes, unreleased status, or benchmark-specific reporting differences, and the paper averages heterogeneous benchmark scores without a principled aggregation or uncertainty estimates.

The ablations are limited to early-stage or reduced 16M settings and do not fully isolate the effects of scale, source data, backbone choice, filtering, relabeling, and benchmark-driven model selection in the final 26M/40M models.

The paper contains overclaiming and marketing-like language, including assertions of state-of-the-art generality, debiased preference representations, and broad alignment significance that are not adequately supported by the experiments.

Ethical and safety discussion is thin given the scale of preference data curation and reward modeling. The paper does not sufficiently address data provenance, consent/licensing, annotator working conditions, or risks from deploying reward models that encode opaque normative preferences.

strengths: The paper studies an important and practically relevant problem: formally verifying neural-network controllers in closed-loop systems with nonlinear dynamics, a setting where many existing tools have clear limitations.

The proposed framework is technically coherent, combining Taylor-model based neural-network approximation, Bernstein polynomial range bounding, domain subdivision, and dReal-based reachability into a plausible sound verification pipeline.
The experiments cover several meaningful benchmark families, including ACC, jet engine control, and TORA, and compare against relevant prior tools such as Verisig, Sherlock, NNV, and ReachNN*.

The reported empirical results are promising, with substantial speedups or larger verified regions in multiple cases, and the paper explores sensitivity to controller size, initial region size, and subdivision choices.
The writing is generally clear, and the paper is well motivated and positioned relative to prior work in neural-network verification and nonlinear reachability.
weaknesses: The technical novelty appears moderate. Many of the core components are established methods, and the paper could more clearly identify what is algorithmically new beyond their integration into a working verifier.

The evaluation does not fully settle scalability: the tested networks and dynamical systems remain relatively modest, with limited evidence for deeper controllers, higher-dimensional plants, or long verification horizons.

Some baseline comparisons are hard to interpret because the tools have different modeling assumptions, precision parameters, solver backends, and timeout/failure modes. More standardized tolerance-runtime comparisons would strengthen the claims.

Reproducibility is a concern: exact benchmark definitions, controller architectures, training details, solver settings, Taylor/Bernstein parameters, and artifact availability are not described in enough detail.
The paper would benefit from stronger ablations isolating the contributions of Taylor order, Bernstein bounding, domain splitting heuristics, and dReal configuration to tightness and runtime.
The practical guidance for choosing subdivision and approximation parameters is limited, yet these choices appear central to both performance and verification success.

strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck in RLHF: reward-model quality appears to be limited substantially by preference-data quality, and the paper makes a timely, practically significant data-centric contribution.

The empirical results are very strong: the proposed Skywork-Reward-V2 models outperform prior open reward models, much larger 70B baselines, and several LLM-as-judge/generative reward-model baselines across seven reward-model benchmarks.

The evaluation is unusually broad for this area, covering general preference accuracy, correctness, safety/harmlessness, style-bias robustness, best-of-N scaling, RewardBench v2, downstream RLHF policy optimization, and an internal human-agreement study.

The ablation suite is convincing overall: the paper studies data quantity vs. quality, filtered vs. corrected labels, human vs. LLM annotation, adaptive retrieval, Stage-2 filtering, and backbone generalization.

The work is likely to be useful to the community if the dataset, attribution/licensing metadata, and model suite are actually released as described. The cost/performance discussion and annotation lessons are also valuable for practitioners.

The paper is generally well written and transparent about several limitations, including subjectivity, dependence on human annotation, ambiguity in discarded/flipped data, and limits of fully automatic curation.
weaknesses: The main novelty is largely in large-scale data curation and engineering rather than a fundamentally new reward-modeling algorithm. The pipeline combines plausible existing ingredients: human verification, LLM-as-judge labeling, retrieval, RM filtering, and consistency checks.

Reproducibility is limited. The best results depend on a very large 40M-pair mixture, many proprietary/frontier LLMs, web/search-enabled annotation, 64 H800 GPUs, and long human annotation cycles. Many implementation details and prompts are deferred to supplementary materials, and independent replication would be difficult.

The definition of “human annotation” is somewhat blurred because annotators are allowed or required to use frontier LLMs, search engines, and domain LLMs. This is pragmatic, but it complicates claims about alignment with human preferences versus agreement with tool-assisted LLM judgments.

The Stage-2 filtering and label flipping rely heavily on reward models trained from earlier curated data, including a “gold RM” treated as an approximation to the true human preference distribution. This could reinforce systematic biases or benchmark-aligned preferences, and the human validation of filtering/flipping appears limited relative to the scale of 40M pairs.

Some evaluation evidence remains internally controlled. The human-agreement benchmark is internal and lacks important details such as sample size, sampling procedure, annotator demographics, inter-annotator agreement, and whether evaluators were blind to model identity.

The dataset is dominated by synthetic prompts/responses and by information-seeking plus coding tasks, with over 95% English data. The claims about broad human preference modeling should therefore be qualified, especially for multilingual, culturally diverse, creative, or highly subjective use cases.

There is residual concern about benchmark overfitting or indirect contamination despite n-gram decontamination, since the pipeline aggregates many public preference sources and uses benchmark-like reward-model feedback during development. The decontamination procedure may not catch semantic or paraphrased overlap.

The ethics and annotation reporting are incomplete and slightly inconsistent: the ethics statement says workers were compensated fairly, while the appendix notes voluntary uncompensated author annotation in later stages. More detail on non-author annotator compensation, demographics, consent, and exposure to harmful content would strengthen the paper.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: open reward models remain brittle, and preference data quality is a plausible bottleneck for RLHF progress.

The empirical headline results are broad and strong: the proposed models outperform prior open reward models across seven reward-model benchmarks, including best-of-N, style-bias, safety, and correctness-oriented evaluations.

The work includes more ablations than many data-scaling papers, including comparisons of uncurated versus curated scaling, human versus LLM curation variants, adaptive retrieval, filtering/flipping, and alternative backbones.
The paper provides useful practical details on dataset composition, training settings, annotation costs, PII analysis, licensing intent, and limitations around subjectivity and preference diversity.
The focus on smaller deployable reward models, rather than only very large 70B-scale models, is practically valuable if the results are reproducible.
weaknesses: The central contribution is largely an engineering/data-curation scale-up rather than a clearly novel algorithmic or scientific advance. The pipeline combines known ingredients: human verification, LLM-as-judge labeling, retrieval, RM consistency filtering, and Bradley-Terry training. The paper does not convincingly isolate a new methodological insight beyond scale and extensive tuning.

The evaluation is vulnerable to benchmark overfitting and data contamination concerns. The dataset is aggregated from many public preference sources, and decontamination is described mostly via n-gram overlap against benchmark prompts, with LLM filtering of false positives. This is not strong enough for a 40M-pair mixture whose sources may contain paraphrases, responses, benchmark-derived examples, or training data from benchmark-adjacent distributions.

The strongest claims rely heavily on public reward-model benchmarks that the authors explicitly optimize against throughout the pipeline. The internal human evaluation and downstream RLHF experiments are comparatively small and under-specified, so they do not fully validate the broad claims about real human preference alignment or downstream utility.

The human annotation protocol is not cleanly human-grounded: annotators are allowed and sometimes required to use frontier LLMs, authors participated in annotation, fewer than 20 annotators were involved over nine months, demographic information is absent, and inter-annotator agreement is not reported in a standard way. This makes the “human preference” signal hard to interpret and may bake in the same model biases the paper aims to correct.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper depends on a very large proprietary-style curation pipeline using many frontier and agentic LLMs, search tools, iterative retrieval, author labor, and 64 H800 training runs. Even with model release, the dataset construction process would be difficult to independently reproduce or audit.

The Stage 2 filtering and flipped-label mechanism is concerning. The method uses reward models trained from earlier stages to decide which labels to keep or flip at massive scale, creating a self-reinforcing loop. The paper gives some human agreement checks, but not enough analysis of systematic false positives, minority preferences, or cases where the gold RM’s biases are amplified.

Several claims are overstated. For example, the paper claims broad versatility, resistance to style bias, and substantial progress in open reward modeling, but the evidence remains largely benchmark-centric and does not establish robustness under adversarial reward hacking, diverse cultural preferences, multi-turn deployment, or real RLHF safety settings.

The dataset is dominated by synthetic English data and by information-seeking plus coding tasks. This weakens claims about nuanced human preferences, multilingual generality, and broad alignment. Subjective, controversial, creative, role-play, planning, and multilingual preferences appear underrepresented.

The ethics and privacy analysis is shallow for a 40M-pair public preference dataset. PII detection relies on LLM scanning, the annotator demographics and working conditions are only briefly described, and the paper does not sufficiently discuss consent, dataset source provenance risks, or misuse of released reward models for reward hacking or unsafe optimization.

The presentation is dense and sometimes promotional. Many tables report large gains, but important experimental details such as sample sizes for human evaluations, exact prompts, filtering thresholds, source-level overlap analysis, statistical uncertainty, and variance across training runs are either deferred, missing, or insufficiently emphasized.

strengths: Important and timely contribution: the paper tackles a central bottleneck in RLHF, namely scalable construction of high-quality preference data, and frames the problem convincingly around the brittleness of current open reward models.

The empirical results are very strong. Skywork-Reward-V2 substantially improves over prior open reward models, larger 70B reward models, LLM-as-judge baselines, and recent generative reward-modeling approaches across a broad seven-benchmark suite.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area, covering general preference benchmarks, correctness-oriented tasks, RewardBench v2, style-bias robustness, best-of-N scaling, downstream RLHF, human agreement, and multiple backbone families.

The paper includes meaningful ablations disentangling data quantity versus curation quality, human annotation versus LLM-only curation, adaptive retrieval, annotation protocols, and Stage 2 filtering; these support the central claim that curation quality, not just scale, drives the gains.

The practical contribution is significant: a large curated preference mixture and a suite of reward models up to 8B parameters could be broadly useful to the open RLHF community if released as described.
The paper is generally well written and provides useful appendix details on dataset composition, decontamination, PII analysis, annotation protocol, training setup, and cost considerations.
weaknesses: The main methodological novelty is partly an engineering synthesis of known ingredients: human verification, LLM-as-judge labeling, retrieval-augmented few-shot annotation, RM filtering, and label flipping. The contribution is compelling at scale, but less algorithmically novel than the performance numbers might suggest.

Reproducibility remains a concern. The pipeline depends on many proprietary/frontier LLMs, evolving agentic models, human annotators, internal validation sets, and a long iterative process over nine months. Even with released data/models, independently reproducing the curation pipeline would be difficult.

Some evaluation evidence risks circularity or selection bias. The same ecosystem of public preference data, LLM judges, and RM-based filtering is used throughout curation, and some human-agreement and downstream RLHF evaluations are internal or lightly specified.

The Stage 2 consistency/filtering procedure may amplify the inductive biases of the gold RM and best RM. The paper provides human-agreement checks, but these are sample-based and do not fully rule out systematic preference narrowing, demographic bias, or overfitting to benchmark-like preference signals.

The paper averages heterogeneous benchmarks into single summary scores without always reporting uncertainty, statistical significance, or sensitivity to benchmark weighting. Given the large claimed margins this may not change the conclusion, but it weakens the rigor of some comparisons.

Dataset ethics and annotation details are helpful but still incomplete: annotator demographics, geographic/cultural coverage, exact compensation context, and the implications of author-volunteer annotation are not fully addressed.

The downstream RLHF evaluation is promising but secondary and relatively limited compared with the extensive benchmark evaluation; more independent policy-training evaluations would strengthen the claim that better RM benchmark scores translate robustly to downstream alignment gains.
